## What peer review does

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
### Transactional

- Vets knowledge
- Gatekeeps
- Routes work to venues
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
### Discursive

- Gives authors feedback
- Sustains argument
- Builds community and mentors
:::
:::

### Where it happens

::: {.muted}
Journals, internal review, friends, open platforms, blogs, journal clubs
:::

::: {.notes}
Two kinds of work happen at once.

- Transactional functions accept, reject, and route
- Discursive functions give feedback, sustain argument, and mentor

It also happens outside journals.

- Internal institutional review
- Informal exchange among friends
- Open platforms such as F1000 and PeerJ
- Blogs and social media
- Journal clubs like this one
:::

## What a good review does

::: {.src}
Buriak et al. 2026, ACS Nano
:::

::: {.lines}
A balanced report that explains its basis

Judgement that tells hype from creative advance

Tone that remembers authors are people, often students
:::

::: {.notes}
**In this section of the editorial**

- Emphasize the scientific value of the work and the basis for the assessment
- Weigh positive and negative aspects, which supports a robust literature and trainee education
- Telling hype from creative advance is a judgement skill the editors place in the human realm
- Authors are often students meeting peer review for the first time, so reread for tone
- Keep requests for new experiments reasonable, since the reviewer is not the research director of the work

**Elsewhere in the editorial**

- On a responsible role for AI, it points to the authors' 2023 editorial on using AI when writing manuscripts, and it rules out using an LLM to check a draft review
- The dangers section lists harms to authors, reviewers, editors, students and early career researchers, and the scientific community, including homogenization of science
- The conclusion accepts that LLMs are widely accessible and asks the community to work out how to use them while protecting peer review
:::

## What LLMs can and cannot do

::: {.src}
Buriak et al. 2026, Figure 1
:::

::: {.check}
| Task | LLM | Human |
|------------------------|--------|--------|
| Research summary | ✓ | ✓ |
| Grammar and spelling | ✓ | ✓ |
| Syntax | ✓ | ✓ |
| Inconsistencies | ✓ | ✓ |
| Novelty assessment | ✗ | ✓ |
| Critical thinking | ✗ | ✓ |
| Experimental logic | ✗ | ✓ |
| Data and graphics analysis | ✗ | ✓ |
:::

::: {.notes}
**Thesis.** Peer review is a human responsibility that cannot be delegated to AI.

- Editors choose a reviewer for their expertise, perspective, and evaluation
- Reports clearly written by generative AI are infrequent but growing
- They are superficial and error prone
- Each one slows the process, because editors have to seek a new reviewer
- The editorial cites a December 2025 survey suggesting more than half of reviewers use AI assistance

**Beyond the figure**

- LLMs trained on existing literature may steamroll imaginative work
- They cannot yet analyze figures or evaluate the primary data in Supporting Information
- They hallucinate citations and data
- The editors doubt any existing LLM will identify breakthroughs or creative insight
:::

## Why AI is entering peer review

::: {.src}
Naddaf 2025, Nature
:::

::: {.lines}
Submissions outgrow the pool of reviewers

Reviewing earns little credit

Reviewers already use AI, often against guidance
:::

::: {.notes}
- Editors struggle to find reviewers
- The Nature report finds more than half of researchers already use AI in peer review, often against guidance
:::

## AI across the review pipeline

::: {.src}
Wu et al. 2026, ACL
:::

::: {.flow}
<span class="step">Review</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Rebuttal</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Meta-review</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Decision</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Revision</span>
:::

::: {.muted}
Methods for generating reviews
:::

::: {.chips}
<span class="chip">Fine-tuning</span><span class="chip">Multi-agent roles</span><span class="chip">Reinforcement learning</span><span class="chip">Retrieval and refinement</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Review is a pipeline, and most work targets its first stage.

- The survey covers generating reviews, rebuttals, and meta-reviews, and revising papers from reviews
- Review generation has received the most attention

**Methods for generating reviews**

- Fine-tuning on corpora of expert reviews
- Multi-agent systems that split a review into roles, such as novelty checking and weakness diagnosis
- Reinforcement learning against rewards for criticism, relevance, and actionability
- Retrieval and iterative refinement to ground the comments
:::

## What is still open

::: {.src}
Wu et al. 2026, ACL
:::

::: {.lines}
Novelty judgement remains weak

Review quality is hard to measure

Evidence comes almost entirely from NLP and ML

Rebuttal, meta-review, and revision are underexplored
:::

::: {.notes}
**Novelty**

- LLMs mimic reviewer tone but stay weak at judging novelty
- Early systems write coherent critiques but cannot tell incremental from groundbreaking work without broader context
- Benchmarks built for novelty assessment show how hard it is

**Evaluation**

- Review quality is hard to quantify, and evaluation often relies on coarse metrics
- The four approaches are human-centric, reference-based (overlap with human-written reviews), LLM-based, and aspect-oriented
- Each trades off scalability, cost, and evaluative depth
- Fine-grained datasets such as ReviewCritique are emerging

**Evidence base**

- Most datasets come from NLP and ML conferences
- Multidisciplinary resources such as MOPRD are a start
- Nobody yet knows whether models overfit to the language of their home domain, and the survey's own limitations section says the same

**Discursive stages**

- Rebuttal, meta-review, and paper revision involve richer discourse and collaborative intent, yet benchmarks are sparse
- Some systems learn from author responses: GoodPoint defines constructive feedback as comments that are both valid and actionable, and RbtAct uses rebuttals as supervision

**Also reported**

- Zero-shot output tends to be generic and overly positive
- Systems are open to manipulation through injection attacks
- LLMs can favour authors from highly ranked institutions in single-blind settings
- The survey closes by calling for explicit disclosure of any LLM use in review
:::

## Accountability laundering

::: {.src}
Pilatti et al. 2026, Ethics & Behavior
:::

::: {.boxes}
::: {.box}
[What the editor sees]{.boxlabel}

A signed, fluent report
:::
::: {.box .unseen}
[What goes unseen]{.boxlabel}

The work behind it
:::
:::

::: {.lines}
The signature keeps its authority while verification weakens
:::

::: {.notes}
**Setup**

- Peer review is a social technology, a pact of trust linking competence, confidentiality, and accountability
- The system sees only the final report
- Generative AI makes plausible, formally organized reports cheap
- Workload, speed, and competition push adoption, which the authors expect to be hard to contain through prohibition alone
- A study cited by Wu et al. estimates that 6.5 to 16.9 percent of review text at top AI venues was substantially modified by LLMs, with use spiking near deadlines and among low-confidence reviews

**Definition**

- The human signature keeps working as a seal of legitimacy
- Its link to the verification the signer actually performed weakens
- A report can look rigorous with generic methodological points and stock limitations, while losing specificity and fit to the manuscript
- The system rewards fluency and rhetorical completeness over verifiable reasons
- The authors call the damage moral and institutional as well as epistemic

**Precondition**

- Effort outsourcing comes first
- The boundary sits where the tool stops being peripheral support and takes over the core of judgement: interpretive summarization, listing limitations, and drafting recommendations
- Buriak et al. make the counterpart point that a computer has no integrity or moral compass and cannot be held accountable

**Method**

- Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with 548 records identified and 10 core sources
- Institutional policies are used as context
- The proposed model is untested, and the paper sets out hypotheses for experimental and field validation
:::

## From writing reviews to checking them

::: {.src}
Pilatti et al. 2026, Ethics & Behavior
:::

::: {.lines}
AI drafts the review

The reviewer checks the draft against the manuscript

The institution audits a sample of reviews

Editors cannot see the reasoning, so audits test the report
:::

::: {.notes}
**The argument**

- GAI reorganizes the cost of cognitive effort. Plausible prose becomes cheap, so central evaluative steps can be outsourced: interpretive summarization, listing limitations, formulating recommendations, even drafting the report
- Those steps sit exactly where diligence is least observable to editors, so they are the most vulnerable to shortcuts
- The result is a quiet change in what counts as reviewing. Plausible prose substitutes for the patient verification that connects comment to evidence and critique to judgement
- The focus moves from the report as a textual product to the review process as a practice of judgement and governance

**The reviewer**

- The role shifts from text production to accountability. The reviewer answers for inferences, relevance, the sufficiency of the reasons, and the prudential choices behind the review
- Any use of AI must be compatible with imputability: the reviewer can answer for every substantive claim, including ones a tool first suggested
- Adversarial threats add a duty, since the reviewer also becomes an element of system security

**The institution**

- Detection is fragile, so governance shifts from policing text to making judgement verifiable
- Disclosure records which tasks AI performed and whether manuscript content was processed
- Auditing samples reports for concrete references to the manuscript, justification of strong recommendations, and unverifiable claims
- The authors expect auditing to reduce the incentive to outsource effort, because it signals that the quality of judgement will be assessed

**The five layers of the model, called Auditable Hybrid Review**

- **Secure infrastructure.** Journal- or institution-controlled environments, with nonretention and nontraining guarantees
- **Granular disclosure.** Record the task, whether manuscript content was processed and where, and any change beyond language polishing
- **AI as signal, not verdict.** Outputs are hypotheses the reviewer must verify and answer for. The paper says this layer targets laundering directly
- **Evidence-anchored auditing.** Sample reports and check their anchoring in the manuscript
- **Adversarial resilience.** Sanitize manuscripts before any AI processing

The paper names three design invariants: confidentiality, accountability, and verifiability. It proposes tiers, from a minimal regime (no external upload, granular disclosure, light auditing) up to private AI environments, so smaller journals can adopt it.

**Trade-offs and tests**

- Effort should move from the reviewer to support systems for mechanical tasks, and reducing workload cannot mean reducing responsibility
- Added friction and bureaucracy could discourage reviewers, so disclosure can be a short checklist and audits can be infrequent, with 5 percent of reports as the authors' example
- Proposed tests include planted errors, to see whether reviewers with AI access verify claims or accept them
:::

## Confidentiality and attack surface

::: {.src}
Buriak et al. 2026; Pilatti et al. 2026
:::

::: {.lines}
Uploading a manuscript to an LLM breaches confidentiality

Detection is fragile, so prohibition pushes use out of sight

Hidden prompts turn the manuscript into an untrusted input
:::

::: {.notes}
**Confidentiality (Buriak et al.)**

- ACS treats uploading a manuscript to an LLM like sharing it with a colleague or friend
- The editors also do not support checking a draft report with an LLM, since a detailed review can indirectly disclose the science in the manuscript
- Intellectual property is a further concern: many LLMs are built by commercial entities with research interests in the same fields, and nobody can know what happens to uploaded material

**Detection and prohibition (Pilatti et al.)**

- Detection is fragile
- Enforcement based on text produces formal compliance and practical opacity
- That pushes use toward external tools, which raises the confidentiality risk

**Adversarial threats (Pilatti et al.)**

- Authors have hidden instructions in manuscripts to influence reviewers' AI tools
- Even reviewers acting in good faith create an attack surface when they run AI on the raw text
:::

## Discussion

::: {.src}
Buriak et al.
:::

::: {.prompt}
A reviewer who reads closely learns from the paper. If AI does the reading, what happens to that learning and to the community it builds?
:::

## Discussion

::: {.src}
Wu et al.
:::

::: {.prompt}
If AI reviews score well against human reviews, does that expose peer review as bureaucracy, or does the comparison miss the discursive function?
:::

## Discussion

::: {.src}
Wu et al.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Does feedback from an AI land differently on the ego than feedback from a peer?
:::

:::
